content: In the field of logic, a contradiction arises when there is a logical incompatibility between two or more propositions. This occurs when the propositions, when considered together, lead to two conclusions that are logical inversions of each other. Beyond formal logic, contradictions can also be identified in actions when their underlying motives are presumed to conflict with one another. In formal logic, particularly in propositional and first-order logic, a proposition φ is considered a contradiction if and only if φ ⊢ ⊥ (where ⊥ represents falsehood). For a contradictory φ, it is true that ⊢ φ → ψ for any ψ (because φ → ⊥ → ψ). This means that any proposition can be proven from a set of axioms that contains contradictions. The method of proof by contradiction is based on the principle that if the negation of a proposition φ (¬φ) leads to a contradiction (¬φ ⊢ ⊥), then φ must be true. This technique is widely used by mathematicians and relies on the logical axiom of the excluded middle (A ∨ ¬A). In mathematical proofs, various symbols are used to denote a contradiction, such as ↯, ⇒ ⇐, ⊥, ↮, and ※. These symbols often appear in proofs by contradiction to indicate that the original assumption was false, thereby affirming the truth of the theorem being proven. In philosophy, adherents of the epistemological theory of coherentism argue that for a belief to be justified, it must be part of a logically consistent system of beliefs. However, some dialetheists, such as Graham Priest, have contended that coherence does not necessarily require consistency. Self-refuting statements and performative contradictions are common in philosophy. These occur when the content or presence of an argument contradicts its own claims. Examples include Heraclitus’s assertion that knowledge is impossible or Nietzsche’s claim that one should not obey others. Such statements undermine themselves by their very nature. Outside formal logic, contradictions can also be identified in colloquial speech. In everyday language, actions or statements may be labeled as contradictory when they are perceived to involve presuppositions that conflict in a logical sense. In dialectics, particularly in Marxism, contradiction refers to the opposition of social forces. According to Karl Marx, capitalism inherently contains contradictions because the social classes within it have conflicting collective goals. These contradictions arise from the social structure of society and inevitably lead to class conflict, economic crises, and ultimately revolution, resulting in the overthrow of the existing order and the rise of the formerly oppressed classes to political power. Mao Zedong expanded on Marx and Lenin’s ideas, proposing that all existence is the result of contradiction.
